analysis.one_liner: Fast-tracks gas pipeline permits and orders completion of the Mountain Valley Pipeline with no court challenges allowed.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Toomey with zero cosponsors on December 1, 2022, never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite three cornerstone environmental laws to speed up pipeline permitting. Under the Clean Water Act, states would get a hard one-year clock to review water quality certifications for pipelines — and if the state missed the deadline, the certification would be deemed waived and construction could proceed. Under the National Environmental Policy Act, environmental impact statements would face 150-page caps and two-year deadlines, and a missed deadline would count as compliance. Under the Endangered Species Act, listing decisions would have to weigh economic impacts on landowners, and the reissuance of nationwide dredge-and-fill permits would be exempt from endangered species consultation entirely. A final section orders federal agencies to reissue every approval needed to finish the Mountain Valley Pipeline in Virginia and West Virginia within 21 days and declares those approvals immune from any court challenge.
analysis.who_benefits: Pipeline developers, above all the companies behind the Mountain Valley Pipeline, which had been stalled for years by permitting fights and court rulings. The bill would hand them a legally mandated set of permits, rewrite the environmental laws that produced those delays, and — uniquely — strip affected parties of any ability to challenge the pipeline's approvals in court. Oil and gas producers generally gain from faster permitting and a narrower definition of protected 'waters of the United States.'

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require federal agencies to reissue all permits, rights-of-way, and biological opinions needed to complete the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 21 days of enactment, copying prior approvals, and it would preempt any statute, regulation, or judicial decision to the contrary.
It would bar any judicial review of any federal approval related to the Mountain Valley Pipeline, removing the court challenges that had repeatedly disrupted the project.

It would impose one-year deadlines on state water quality certifications, with a missed deadline meaning the certification requirement is waived, and state-issued permits deemed approved if the state fails to act within a year.

It would cap environmental impact statements at 150 pages (300 for complex projects), require completion within two years with a missed deadline deemed to satisfy the law, and cut endangered species consultation timelines from 90 days to 60 days.

It would force the Army Corps of Engineers to maintain a nationwide permit covering oil and gas pipeline construction and exempt that permit's reissuance from both Endangered Species Act consultation and detailed environmental review.
It would narrow the definition of protected waters to exclude ephemeral streams and many wetlands, reducing the stream and wetland crossings subject to federal permitting.

analysis.who_pays: Communities along pipeline routes, including landowners, would lose their day in court: the bill's signature provision bars all judicial review of Mountain Valley Pipeline approvals. States lose authority — the bill limits what a state may consider in a water quality certification to water-quality compliance alone, voids conditions it disfavors, and lets federal agencies overrule state review timelines. Weakened environmental review under NEPA and the Endangered Species Act spreads across all major federal projects, and the narrower 'waters of the United States' definition leaves more streams and wetlands unprotected for everyone, not just pipelines.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let a federal permitting agency treat a missed environmental review deadline as satisfying the law, and let pipeline projects be deemed approved if a state misses its own deadline — trading review quality for speed.

It would add economic impacts on landowners as a required factor in deciding whether a species is listed as endangered, a change conservation supporters argue could block protection for imperiled species.

It would exempt the reissuance of nationwide dredge-and-fill permits from Endangered Species Act consultation and from a full environmental impact statement, meaning individual pipeline crossings across hundreds of streams would face no species-by-species review.

Its final section would prohibit any court from reviewing federal approvals for the Mountain Valley Pipeline — a one-project carve-out that removes accountability for a specific private project and would prevent affected landowners from challenging permits in court.

Defenders of permitting reform argue genuine delays are real: some environmental reviews drag on for years and litigation adds more time, and supporters contend faster permitting lowers energy costs and strengthens energy security — the bill's title frames it that way. But this bill went well beyond general streamlining to target one specific pipeline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some general permitting-streamlining ideas here (page limits, deadlines, categorical exclusions across agencies) echo bipartisan reform proposals and are not inherently one-sided. But the bill's center of gravity is Section 5: a legally mandated, court-proof completion of one named pipeline, plus a rewrite of the Clean Water Act, NEPA, and the Endangered Species Act that removes deadlines' teeth in favor of industry and leaves states and courts with far less say. For ordinary people the costs — lost legal standing, weakened water and species protections, a narrower shield for streams and wetlands — outweigh modest energy-price benefits, and the law would be written around one private project's needs.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors on December 1, 2022, it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and no committee vote or floor action ever followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Toomey (R-PA) introduced the Pipeline Permitting for Energy Security Act of 2022 in the Senate on December 1, 2022.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it stayed; no further action was taken.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no hearing in the record before then.

Under Senate rules, a bill referred to committee generally cannot reach the floor until the committee reports it out, so without committee action the bill expired automatically at the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the environmental review and water-quality protections it would have weakened remain intact for the 117th Congress, and no pipeline was exempted from judicial review. The companies behind the Mountain Valley Pipeline did not receive the guaranteed permits and litigation immunity this bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landowners and communities near pipeline routes

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 1, 2022 and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it remained stalled in committee from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and it died without any vote in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline developers (Mountain Valley Pipeline partners)
industries.note: Section 5 would have ordered every federal approval needed to finish the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 21 days and barred all court review of those approvals — a direct legal guarantee for a specific stalled project. Landowners and communities along the route would have lost the ability to challenge permits.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would speed Clean Water Act certifications, cap and weaken NEPA reviews, expedite endangered species consultations, narrow which waters are federally protected, and mandate a nationwide permit for pipeline stream crossings — all reducing permitting friction industry had long sought.

industries.industry: State water quality and environmental agencies
industries.note: The bill would restrict what states may consider in water quality certifications, void certification conditions after federal review, deem applications approved when states miss deadlines, and preempt inconsistent law — stripping state authority over pipeline water impacts.

industries.industry: Construction and engineering contractors on major federal projects
industries.note: Shorter, capped environmental reviews would cut delay costs on some projects, but deemed-approved deadlines and forfeited-comment rules also add compliance risk and litigation exposure under compressed timelines.
